**Start with the supplied agent, get one complete negotiation working, then improve its data preparation and offer selection.** The competition rewards total deal value, so better evidence and reliable calculations are likely to matter more than a complicated agent architecture.

I read the repository’s brief, starter instructions, data guide and submission requirements. The arena website itself wasn’t accessible through my browsing tool.

This is also an important addition to our earlier research: **Tacto has published an MIT-licensed buyer starter kit and local simulator. Its actual supplier agents remain hosted.** [Official repository](https://github.com/tacto-ai/negotiation-arena-kit).

**1. Get a working baseline**

You need Git, Python 3.12 and `uv`.

```bash
git clone https://github.com/tacto-ai/negotiation-arena-kit.git
cd negotiation-arena-kit/starter-kit
uv sync --all-extras
cp .env.example .env
```

Apply for your team key at [the application page](https://arena.tacto.ai/apply), show your match code at the Tacto table, and copy the key into `.env` as `ARENA_API_KEY`. Keep it out of Git and Discord.

Then run:

```bash
uv run arena me
uv run arena cases
uv run arena play case:P01 -v
```

Your first goal is simply to finish a case and inspect its score and replay. [Setup instructions](https://github.com/tacto-ai/negotiation-arena-kit#start-in-15-minutes).

**No key yet?** Run the local simulator in one terminal:

```bash
uv run arena-sim serve --no-clock
```

In a second terminal:

```bash
ARENA_URL=http://127.0.0.1:8000 uv run arena register "Hello World" sim
```

Use the simulator key it prints:

```bash
ARENA_URL=http://127.0.0.1:8000 ARENA_API_KEY=<simulator-key> uv run arena play case:S01 -v
```

The simulator checks your integration; its scripted supplier won’t teach you the hosted opponents’ negotiation strategies. [Local walkthrough](https://github.com/tacto-ai/negotiation-arena-kit/blob/main/starter-kit/README.md#hello-world-local-3-commands).

**2. Understand what wins before changing the agent**

The accepted deal is evaluated across a fixed need and time horizon. Its cost includes price, uncovered demand, payment timing, freight, delivery delays, quality and other applicable terms. Certain strategic cases also penalize leaving the supplier with an unsustainable margin.

**A lower unit price can produce a worse score** if the contract covers too little demand or has unfavorable other terms. Breaking a must-have scores zero; walking away can be the correct choice. [Scoring rules](https://github.com/tacto-ai/negotiation-arena-kit/blob/main/brief/brief.md#6-the-score-total-cost-in-).

My recommendation: make the published `total_cost` function your offer evaluator. Let code calculate and validate; let the model interpret the supplier and write the email.

**3. Build a short preparation file for every case**

Before opening negotiations, collect:

| Context | Where to look |
|---|---|
| Previous prices and concessions | `price_conditions`, `negotiation_history` |
| Supplier reliability | `scorecards`, delivery and quality records |
| Existing obligations | Contracts and clauses |
| Supplier interests | Correspondence, call notes, news |
| Cost evidence | `cost_drivers`, `index_values`, `should_cost` |
| Buyer behavior | Forecast accuracy and invoice/payment history |

Retain the evidence IDs alongside each finding. Check price units carefully: some prices are per 100 or 1,000 pieces, or per kg/metre. [Data guide](https://github.com/tacto-ai/negotiation-arena-kit/blob/main/data/README.md).

A useful preparation summary is:

> Our objective; mandatory terms; best alternative; strongest relevant evidence; likely supplier interests; tradeable terms; unresolved questions.

**4. Improve three decisions first**

These are my suggested implementation priorities:

- **What to ask:** request information that could change your next offer—cost breakdown, capacity, delivery schedule or approval requirements.
- **What to offer:** generate two or three packages trading price against payment, duration or other allowed terms; calculate each package’s total cost.
- **When to close:** compare valid standing offers with your alternative and remaining time. Don’t lose an acceptable deal while chasing a marginal improvement.

For example, a supplier concerned about cash might prefer faster payment for a price reduction. A supplier with limited authority over price might move on delivery or another term.

**Emails alone do not bind the deal: structured term sheets do.** Explicitly accept a supplier’s standing term-sheet ID to close. An `agreed` response still requires your acceptance. [API contract](https://github.com/tacto-ai/negotiation-arena-kit/blob/main/brief/api.md).

**5. Practice with a controlled learning loop**

Configure your model using the starter README, download the data, then try:

```bash
uv run arena data
uv run arena play case:P01 --agent llm -v
```

After each run, inspect:

- Which cost component improved or worsened?
- Which argument was verified, irrelevant or contradicted?
- What did the supplier reveal about its priorities?
- Did your closing decision preserve the best available outcome?

Change one behavior at a time and compare results. You have **200 practice sessions per rolling 24 hours**, so reserve sessions for final rehearsal. Your own agent implements `decide(case, threads)`; retain the starter client and runner initially. [Starter guide](https://github.com/tacto-ai/negotiation-arena-kit/blob/main/starter-kit/README.md).

**6. Prepare for Sunday**

For this weekend, Sunday is **11 October**. The published schedule calls for refreshing data after **08:00**, a pre-flight at **09:00**, and code/submission freeze at **12:00**.

Start the supplied final runner before noon:

```bash
uv run arena run --set final --agent llm --parallel 10
```

That command runs the starter LLM agent; adapt the integration when using your implementation. Submit your accessible repository, running commit hash, approach description and slides. During the final, no human intervention or agent access to the prohibited live feeds is allowed. Keep the machine powered and awake. [Submission checklist](https://github.com/tacto-ai/negotiation-arena-kit/blob/main/brief/submission.md).

**Your first milestone should be one completed hosted case with a replay you can explain: why you chose each argument, what you traded, and why you accepted or walked away.**

"""Play cases with an agent against the arena over HTTP - the hosted arena (practice, sandbox,
final) or `arena-sim`, the local contract simulator. Both speak the same API.

An agent is any object with `decide(case, threads) -> {"supplier_id": ..., "message": {...}}`:
  threads: {supplier_id: [message, ...]} - every e-mail so far, both directions, in order;
           supplier attachments carry their text under "text" (see `docs.read_document`).
  message: subject, body, up to 3 term sheets, refs - or an "action" that closes the case:
           {"type": "accept", "term_sheet_id": ...} or {"type": "walk_away"}.
"""

import functools
import logging
import re
import threading
import time
from concurrent.futures import ThreadPoolExecutor

from .client import ArenaError
from .cost import must_haves_ok, total_cost
from .docs import read_document, standard_terms

log = logging.getLogger("arena")

ENDED = {"walked_away", "no_bid"}
# A message later than this after the supplier's last one counts as a timeout.
MOVE_LIMIT_S = 60
# In the Live Final, close this long before the wave's cap - or the slowest round of the case so far
# (your decision plus a supplier reply of up to about a minute) plus a margin, if that is longer.
CLOSE_BEFORE_CAP_S, ROUND_MARGIN_S = 90, 15
RUNNING = re.compile(r"one session per case in the final: (\S+)")
# Practice: the case list shows every practice case file; only those marked hosted can be played
# (a session on another is a 403). Without the marker every listed case counts as hosted.
HOSTED_FIELD = "hosted"


class RemoteTable:
    """The arena over HTTP: the practice arena, the final, or a hosted sandbox."""

"""The naive buyer: anchors a little low, splits the difference, accepts early.

A baseline to beat, not a strategy: it ignores the data and the documents, never trades, never
asks and never walks away. One term sheet per e-mail.
"""

from ..cost import complete_offer, total_cost
from ..play import latest, live_threads, moves_left, standing


class NaiveAgent:
    def __init__(self, anchor=0.10, close_gap=0.01):
        self.anchor, self.close_gap = anchor, close_gap

`starter-kit/` is a small Python package, `arena_kit`, of about 2,700 lines including tests. It plays your buyer against the arena's supplier agents and calculates deal cost in code. I read the module headers and function lists, not every line.

## How the pieces connect

The `arena` command line (`cli.py`) loads `.env` and builds an agent. It then hands it to `play.py`, which loops: fetch the case, call `agent.decide(case, threads)`, send the move over HTTP via `client.py`, and repeat until a deal, a walk-away or a timeout. The same loop runs against the hosted arena or the local simulator, because both speak the same API.

## Files in `arena_kit/`

| File | Role |
|---|---|
| `play.py` | The game loop. `RemoteTable` is the HTTP session. `play_all` runs cases in parallel and `play_waves` runs the final. It also has the helpers `standing`, `latest`, `live_threads` and `moves_left`. |
| `agents/llm.py` | The LLM buyer, and the file you'll edit most. |
| `agents/naive.py` | A baseline that anchors 10% low, splits the difference and accepts early. It ignores the data. |
| `cost.py` | The published cost function. `total_cost` is the score you want to minimise, and `must_haves_ok` checks hard constraints. `complete_offer` and `snap` fill and round term sheets, and `supplier_value` and `relationship_cost` price an unsustainable supplier margin. |
| `data.py` | Read-only access to the data package: SQL queries, lookup by citable ID (`po:…`, `idx:…`) and documents. |
| `docs.py` | Turns attached PDFs and XLSX files into text. It also parses a supplier's quote PDF into structured standard terms. |
| `client.py` | The HTTP client. It retries safely with a move ID, paces calls to about 9 a second, and tracks your practice quota. |
| `mcp_server.py` | An optional read-only MCP server over the data, so another agent framework can explore it. |
| `sim.py` and `sim_cases/` | The local simulator with scripted suppliers (cases `S01` to `S03`). It's the biggest file at 725 lines. |

`tests/` holds the kit's own tests, and `.env.example`, `Dockerfile` and `pyproject.toml` hold config. Your CLAUDE.md says no smoke tests, which applies to tests you add.

## How the LLM agent decides

The code in `llm.py` does the numbers and the model does the talking:

1. **Prepare:** it gathers the case, the data rows the case points to, and each standing term sheet's cost from `total_cost`. It also reads the supplier's quote PDF for standard terms.
2. **Model call:** the model returns one JSON object. That's either a message with up to three term sheets, or `accept`, or `walk_away`.
3. **Guard:** code fills and rounds the term sheets and strips any cited data ID that doesn't exist, since an unknown ID costs trust. It refuses an accept that breaks a must-have or loses to the alternative.

The agent only sees what the case file points to. Finding other evidence that moves a supplier is left to you, which is where your preparation step fits.

## Where to improve it

Your plan has three decisions: what to ask, what to offer, and when to close. They map to `SYSTEM` and `render` for the prompt and evidence, `prepare` and `fact` for pulling extra data through `data.py`, and `guard` plus `cost.py` for offer selection and closing. I'd start with the evidence step, since the agent currently sees only what the case file points to.

# Workflow authoring reference

A workflow structures work across many agents — to be comprehensive (decompose and cover in parallel), to be confident (independent perspectives and adversarial checks before committing), or to take on scale one context can't hold (migrations, audits, broad sweeps). The script is where you encode that structure: what fans out, what verifies, what synthesizes.

When you do call it, the right move is often **hybrid**: scout inline first (list the files, find the channels, scope the diff) to discover the work-list, then call Workflow to pipeline over it. You don't need to know the shape before the *task* — only before the *orchestration step*.

Common single-phase workflows you can chain across turns:
- **Understand** — parallel readers over relevant subsystems → structured map
- **Design** — judge panel of N independent approaches → scored synthesis
- **Review** — dimensions → find → adversarially verify (the review-changes example)
- **Research** — multi-modal sweep → deep-read → synthesize
- **Migrate** — discover sites → transform each (worktree isolation) → verify

For larger work, run several in sequence — read each result before deciding the next phase. You stay in the loop; each workflow is one well-scoped fan-out.

**Ultracode.** When a system-reminder confirms ultracode is on, that opt-in is standing: author and run a workflow for every substantive task by default. The goal is the most exhaustive, correct answer you can produce — token cost is not a constraint. For multi-phase work (understand → design → implement → review), that often means several workflows in sequence — one per phase — so you stay in the loop between them. The quality patterns below (adversarial verify, multi-modal sweep, completeness critic, loop-until-dry) are the tools; pick what fits the task. Lean toward orchestrating with workflows and adversarially verifying your findings — unless the work is trivial or already verified. Solo only on conversational turns or trivial mechanical edits. When a reminder says ultracode is off, revert to the opt-in rule in the Workflow tool description.

Pass the script inline via `script` — do not Write it to a file first. Every invocation automatically persists its script to a file under the session directory and returns the path in the tool result. To iterate on a workflow, edit that file with Write/Edit and re-invoke Workflow with `{scriptPath: "<path>"}` instead of resending the full script.

Every script must begin with `export const meta = {...}`:
  export const meta = {
    name: 'find-flaky-tests',
    description: 'Find flaky tests and propose fixes',   // one-line, shown in permission dialog
    phases: [                                            // one entry per phase() call
      { title: 'Scan', detail: 'grep test logs for retries' },
      { title: 'Fix', detail: 'one agent per flaky test' },
    ],
  }
  // script body starts here — use agent()/parallel()/pipeline()/phase()/log()
  phase('Scan')
  const flaky = await agent('grep CI logs for retry markers', {schema: FLAKY_SCHEMA})
  ...

The `meta` object must be a PURE LITERAL — no variables, function calls, spreads, or template interpolation. Required fields: `name`, `description`. Optional: `whenToUse` (shown in the workflow list), `phases`. Use the SAME phase titles in meta.phases as in phase() calls — titles are matched exactly; a phase() call with no matching meta entry just gets its own progress group. Add `model` to a phase entry when that phase uses a specific model override.

Script body hooks:
- agent(prompt: string, opts?: {label?: string, phase?: string, schema?: object, model?: string, effort?: string, isolation?: 'worktree', agentType?: string}): Promise<any> — spawn a subagent. Without schema, returns its final text as a string. With schema (a JSON Schema), the subagent is forced to call a StructuredOutput tool and agent() returns the validated object — no parsing needed. Returns null if the user skips the agent mid-run or the subagent dies on a terminal API error after retries (filter with .filter(Boolean)). opts.label overrides the display label. opts.phase explicitly assigns this agent to a progress group (use this inside pipeline()/parallel() stages to avoid races on the global phase() state — same phase string → same group box). opts.model overrides the model for this agent call. Default to omitting it — the agent inherits the main-loop model (the resolved session model), which is almost always correct. Only set it when you're highly confident a different tier fits the task; when unsure, omit. opts.effort overrides the reasoning effort for this agent call ('low' | 'medium' | 'high' | 'xhigh' | 'max') — omit to inherit the session effort; use 'low' for cheap mechanical stages and higher tiers only for the hardest verify/judge stages. opts.isolation: 'worktree' runs the agent in a fresh git worktree — EXPENSIVE (~200-500ms setup + disk per agent), use ONLY when agents mutate files in parallel and would otherwise conflict; the worktree is auto-removed if unchanged. opts.agentType uses a custom subagent type (e.g. 'general-purpose', 'code-reviewer') instead of the default workflow subagent — resolved from the same registry as the Agent tool; composes with schema (the custom agent's system prompt gets a StructuredOutput instruction appended).
- pipeline(items, stage1, stage2, ...): Promise<any[]> — run each item through all stages independently, NO barrier between stages. Item A can be in stage 3 while item B is still in stage 1. This is the DEFAULT for multi-stage work. Wall-clock = slowest single-item chain, not sum-of-slowest-per-stage. Every stage callback receives (prevResult, originalItem, index) — use originalItem/index in later stages to label work without threading context through stage 1's return value. A stage that throws drops that item to `null` and skips its remaining stages.
- parallel(thunks: Array<() => Promise<any>>): Promise<any[]> — run tasks concurrently. This is a BARRIER: awaits all thunks before returning. A thunk that throws (or whose agent errors) resolves to `null` in the result array — the call itself never rejects, so `.filter(Boolean)` before using the results. Use ONLY when you genuinely need all results together.
- log(message: string): void — emit a progress message to the user (shown as a narrator line above the progress tree)
- phase(title: string): void — start a new phase; subsequent agent() calls are grouped under this title in the progress display
- args: any — the value passed as Workflow's `args` input, verbatim (undefined if not provided). Pass arrays/objects as actual JSON values in the tool call, NOT as a JSON-encoded string — `args: ["a.ts", "b.ts"]`, not `args: "[\"a.ts\", ...]"` (a stringified list reaches the script as one string, so `args.filter`/`args.map` throw). Use this to parameterize named workflows — e.g. pass a research question, target path, or config object directly instead of via a side-channel file.
- budget: {total: number|null, spent(): number, remaining(): number} — the turn's token target from the user's "+500k"-style directive. `budget.total` is null if no target was set. `budget.spent()` returns output tokens spent this turn across the main loop and all workflows — the pool is shared, not per-workflow. `budget.remaining()` returns `max(0, total - spent())`, or `Infinity` if no target. The target is a HARD ceiling, not advisory: once `spent()` reaches `total`, further `agent()` calls throw. Use for dynamic loops: `while (budget.total && budget.remaining() > 50_000) { ... }`, or static scaling: `const FLEET = budget.total ? Math.floor(budget.total / 100_000) : 5`.
- workflow(nameOrRef: string | {scriptPath: string}, args?: any): Promise<any> — run another workflow inline as a sub-step and return whatever it returns. Pass a name to invoke a saved workflow (same registry as {name: "..."}), or {scriptPath} to run a script file you Wrote earlier. The child shares this run's concurrency cap, agent counter, abort signal, and token budget — its agents appear under a "▸ name" group in /workflows and its tokens count toward budget.spent(). The args param becomes the child's `args` global. Nesting is one level only: workflow() inside a child throws. Throws on unknown name / unreadable scriptPath / child syntax error; catch to handle gracefully.

Subagents are told their final text IS the return value (not a human-facing message), so they return raw data. For structured output, use the schema option — validation happens at the tool-call layer so the model retries on mismatch.
Schemas need {type: 'object', properties: {...}} at root and required ⊆ properties; unsatisfiable ones throw at agent().

Workflow agents can reach all session-connected MCP tools via ToolSearch — schemas load on demand per agent. Caveat: interactively-authenticated MCP servers (e.g. claude.ai) may be absent in headless/cron runs.

Subagents get the same CLAUDE.md files injected at start that you did (except built-in agent types that omit them, such as Explore and Plan) — don't tell them to re-read those or paste their rules into the prompt; name the specific rule a stage needs, if any.

Scripts are plain JavaScript, NOT TypeScript — type annotations (`: string[]`), interfaces, and generics fail to parse. The script body runs in an async context — use await directly. Standard JS built-ins (JSON, Math, Array, etc.) are available — EXCEPT `Date.now()`/`Math.random()`/argless `new Date()`, which throw (they would break resume); pass timestamps in via `args`, stamp results after the workflow returns, and for randomness vary the agent prompt/label by index. No filesystem or Node.js API access.

DEFAULT TO pipeline(). Only reach for a barrier (parallel between stages) when you genuinely need ALL prior-stage results together.

A barrier is correct ONLY when stage N needs cross-item context from all of stage N-1:
- Dedup/merge across the full result set before expensive downstream work
- Early-exit if the total count is zero ("0 bugs found → skip verification entirely")
- Stage N's prompt references "the other findings" for comparison

A barrier is NOT justified by:
- "I need to flatten/map/filter first" — do it inside a pipeline stage: pipeline(items, stageA, r => transform([r]).flat(), stageB)
- "The stages are conceptually separate" — that's what pipeline() models. Separate stages ≠ synchronized stages.
- "It's cleaner code" — barrier latency is real. If 5 finders run and the slowest takes 3× the fastest, a barrier wastes 2/3 of the fast finders' idle time.

Smell test: if you wrote
  const a = await parallel(...)
  const b = transform(a)        // flatten, map, filter — no cross-item dependency
  const c = await parallel(b.map(...))
that middle transform doesn't need the barrier. Rewrite as a pipeline with the transform inside a stage. When in doubt: pipeline.

Concurrent agent() calls are capped at min(16, available CPUs - 2) per workflow — excess calls queue and run as slots free up. You can still pass 100 items to parallel()/pipeline() and they all complete; only ~10 run at any moment. Total agent count across a workflow's lifetime is capped at 1000 — a runaway-loop backstop set far above any real workflow. A single parallel()/pipeline() call accepts at most 4096 items; passing more is an explicit error, not a silent truncation.

When a barrier IS correct — dedup across all findings before expensive verification:
  const all = await parallel(DIMENSIONS.map(d => () => agent(d.prompt, {schema: FINDINGS_SCHEMA})))
  const deduped = dedupeByFileAndLine(all.filter(Boolean).flatMap(r => r.findings))  // <-- genuinely needs ALL at once
  const verified = await parallel(deduped.map(f => () => agent(verifyPrompt(f), {schema: VERDICT_SCHEMA})))

Loop-until-count pattern — accumulate to a target:
  const bugs = []
  while (bugs.length < 10) {
    const result = await agent("Find bugs in this codebase.", {schema: BUGS_SCHEMA})
    bugs.push(...result.bugs)
    log(`${bugs.length}/10 found`)
  }

Loop-until-budget pattern — scale depth to the user's "+500k" directive. Guard on budget.total: with no target set, remaining() is Infinity and the loop would run straight to the 1000-agent cap.
  const bugs = []
  while (budget.total && budget.remaining() > 50_000) {
    const result = await agent("Find bugs in this codebase.", {schema: BUGS_SCHEMA})
    bugs.push(...result.bugs)
    log(`${bugs.length} found, ${Math.round(budget.remaining()/1000)}k remaining`)
  }

Composing patterns — exhaustive review (find → dedup vs seen → diverse-lens panel → loop-until-dry):
  const seen = new Set(), confirmed = []
  let dry = 0
  while (dry < 2) {                                              // loop-until-dry
    const found = (await parallel(FINDERS.map(f => () =>          // barrier: collect all finders this round
      agent(f.prompt, {phase: 'Find', schema: BUGS})))).filter(Boolean).flatMap(r => r.bugs)
    const fresh = found.filter(b => !seen.has(key(b)))           // dedup vs ALL seen — plain code, not an agent
    if (!fresh.length) { dry++; continue }
    dry = 0; fresh.forEach(b => seen.add(key(b)))
    const judged = await parallel(fresh.map(b => () =>           // every fresh bug judged concurrently...
      parallel(['correctness','security','repro'].map(lens => () =>   // ...each by 3 distinct lenses
        agent(`Judge "${b.desc}" via the ${lens} lens — real?`, {phase: 'Verify', schema: VERDICT})))
        .then(vs => ({ b, real: vs.filter(Boolean).filter(v => v.real).length >= 2 }))))
    confirmed.push(...judged.filter(v => v.real).map(v => v.b))
  }
  return confirmed
  // dedup vs `seen`, NOT `confirmed` — else judge-rejected findings reappear every round and it never converges.

Quality patterns — common shapes; pick by task and compose freely:
- Adversarial verify: spawn N independent skeptics per finding, each prompted to REFUTE. Kill if ≥majority refute. Prevents plausible-but-wrong findings from surviving.
    const votes = await parallel(Array.from({length: 3}, () => () =>
      agent(`Try to refute: ${claim}. Default to refuted=true if uncertain.`, {schema: VERDICT})))
    const survives = votes.filter(Boolean).filter(v => !v.refuted).length >= 2
- Perspective-diverse verify: when a finding can fail in more than one way, give each verifier a distinct lens (correctness, security, perf, does-it-reproduce) instead of N identical refuters — diversity catches failure modes redundancy can't.
- Judge panel: generate N independent attempts from different angles (e.g. MVP-first, risk-first, user-first), score with parallel judges, synthesize from the winner while grafting the best ideas from runners-up. Beats one-attempt-iterated when the solution space is wide.
- Loop-until-dry: for unknown-size discovery (bugs, issues, edge cases), keep spawning finders until K consecutive rounds return nothing new. Simple counters (while count < N) miss the tail.
- Multi-modal sweep: parallel agents each searching a different way (by-container, by-content, by-entity, by-time). Each is blind to what the others surface; useful when one search angle won't find everything.
- Completeness critic: a final agent that asks "what's missing — modality not run, claim unverified, source unread?" What it finds becomes the next round of work.
- No silent caps: if a workflow bounds coverage (top-N, no-retry, sampling), `log()` what was dropped — silent truncation reads as "covered everything" when it didn't.

Scale to what the user asked for. "find any bugs" → a few finders, single-vote verify. "thoroughly audit this" or "be comprehensive" → larger finder pool, 3–5 vote adversarial pass, synthesis stage. When unsure, lean toward thoroughness for research/review/audit requests and toward brevity for quick checks.

These patterns aren't exhaustive — compose novel harnesses when the task calls for it (tournament brackets, self-repair loops, staged escalation, whatever fits).

Use this tool for multi-step orchestration where control flow should be deterministic (loops, conditionals, fan-out) rather than model-driven.

## Resume

The tool result includes a runId. To resume after a pause, kill, or script edit, relaunch with Workflow({scriptPath, resumeFromRunId}) — the longest unchanged prefix of agent() calls returns cached results instantly; the first edited/new call and everything after it runs live. Same script + same args → 100% cache hit. Before diagnosing why a completed workflow returned an empty or unexpected result, Read <transcriptDir>/journal.jsonl — it records each agent's actual return value; do not assume cached results are non-empty. Date.now()/Math.random()/new Date() are unavailable in scripts (they would break this) — stamp results after the workflow returns, or pass timestamps via args. Fallback when no journal is available: Read agent-<id>.jsonl files in the transcript directory and hand-author a continuation script.

## 1. Challenge and data

**Docs and data**

- The data package is the repo-root `data/` folder. It is read through `ARENA_DATA` (`starter-kit/README.md:38`, `AK/cli.py:62`) [C].

**Cases and goals**
- Case types are price_increase, renewal, rfq, bundling, raw_material, capacity and quality (`brief/api.md:312`) [C].
- An RFQ has 2-3 supplier threads, and accepting one ends the case [C].
- Category goals are stabilise, secure_supply, quality_first, leverage and routine. The goal sets the rates (`api.md:332-335`, `AK/cost.py:15-16`) [C].

- C = spend + uncovered need at the fallback price × (1 + risk) + payment-term interest + freight + late cost + defect cost + tooling + index adjustment and risk + relationship.
- Payment interest is `spend*r*(d_ref-payment_days)/360`.
- A contract shorter than the horizon pushes the uncovered need to the fallback price.
- I recomputed S03 with `cost.total_cost` at 217.77, 60 days and FCA. 12 months costs 4,118,431 and 24 months costs 3,771,767, so 12 months is about 347k worse. This matches the brief's "same price for 12 months scores worse than opening" (`brief.md:154-160`).

## 3. Proposed architecture

Keep the stack. Add a small deterministic layer around one LLM call per turn. Do not build a multi-agent framework and do not add a separate Closer role.

| Role | Type | Input | Output |
|---|---|---|---|
| Prepare (once per case) | Deterministic SQL, optionally one LLM summary | case, `DataPackage` | Dossier: evidence cards `{id, fact, figure}` (only IDs whose record holds a figure), justified-move calc, one supplier cost estimate for the relationship term |
| Strategy, terms and message (per turn) | One LLM call, 25-30 s timeout | Dossier, thread events, candidate packages (seeds), previous `notes` | JSON: `term_sheets` (validated by code), `claims` as `{id, figure}`, `body`, free-text `notes`, optional approval/role flag |
| Evaluate and validate | Deterministic | proposed sheets, standing sheets, case | C including the relationship term, must-haves, no-regression, claim cap, dedupe and figure tolerance, leak check |
| Accept or walk | Deterministic, one shared `accept_ok(case, threads, sid)` | standing sheets, alternative | used by `closing_move`, `guard` and `NaiveAgent` |

**State**
- State stays in `threads` (the events list). Used claims and pushed-after-final are derived by small pure helpers, not a second `Ledger` store.
- The only new memory is the LLM's `notes` string, fed back next turn.
- Offer history is built from the arena's thread data. Late sends are not recorded as offers.

**Handoffs**
- The ranker only seeds candidates in the prompt.
- The LLM proposes terms and code validates them with `complete_offer`, must-haves, no-regression and a price floor.
- Claims are rendered from the Dossier in code, so the figure always matches the fact row.
- The single fallback is `NaiveAgent` hardened with `accept_ok`. It is precomputed before the LLM call.

### One negotiation turn
1. `play()` gets the reply, fetches attachments and parses standard terms (`play.py:142-181`).
2. Re-read `seconds_left` and the per-thread deadline (about 35 s from the supplier reply).
3. If near the cap, run `closing_move` using `accept_ok`.
4. Precompute the fallback move and the ranked seed packages (C with the relationship estimate).
5. If `accept_ok` is satisfied and status is `final_offer`, or rounds are nearly out, send accept.
6. Call the LLM with the allow-listed case view, the Dossier, the seeds, the events and the previous `notes`. Expect JSON.
7. Validate:
   - sheets are complete and valid;
   - no must-have breach;
   - no regression against our previous sheet or the supplier's;
   - at most 3 claims, each ID in the Dossier and not repeated;
   - no leaked limits.
8. On failure or timeout, send the precomputed fallback.
9. Send. On 422, resend the deterministic sheet. On a late 409, record a timeout, not an offer. Loop.

**RFQ**: run one worker per thread (or send each round concurrently) so thread B's clock does not run out while A is served. Never accept before comparing all live sheets.

## 4. Negotiation behavior

- **Interest inference**:
  - Compute the justified cost move from drivers × idx changes.
  - Use the supplier performance gap (`sc`, `qn`), volume stability (`fc`) and cash sensitivity (`credit_index`, `equity_ratio`, `skonto_*`, late payments).
  - Use the settled-versus-asked pattern and correspondence themes.
  - Treat all of these as ranked hypotheses [A]. The LLM states them in `notes`.
- **Tone**: do not model emotions. Track observable signals (status, `final_offer`, timeouts, concession per round, reply delay). Keep the tone neutral, factual and short.
- **Stabilise and secure_supply**: use the relationship estimate as an advisory price floor until hosted practice validates it. Its source is a `should_cost` row or a `cost_drivers`-based estimate. Provide it through one `total_cost` wrapper used at every call site.
- **Packages**: send 2-3 sheets enumerated from `term_options` and ranked by C. Examples are price/payment pairs, longer contract at lower price, and incoterm swaps. Offer cheap-for-us items (volume visibility, 30-day payment) for a larger price move.
- **Roles and approvals**: no thresholds are documented (`brief.md:38-46`) [A]. The LLM flags a role or approval request in `notes` and re-engages with whoever replies. No deterministic rule until replays show a pattern.
- **Accept**:
  - The standing sheet must be the lowest C among live threads.
  - Must-haves must pass on the closing terms.
  - C must be below C_alt, with a margin.
  - There must be no missing fields, or the fill-ins must be priced.
  - Either status is `final_offer` or rounds are nearly out.
- **Walk**: walk when no sheet passes. Make `closing_move` choose the walking thread deliberately and not `live_threads()[0]` (`play.py:138`), which ends a whole RFQ.
- **Privacy**:
  - Build the prompt from an allow-listed case view, not `json.dumps(case)`.
  - Add output checks for numbers equal to C_alt, the budget or the rates.
  - Do not cite rival quotes unless the leak is intended.

**Priority order**
1. **Baseline hardening (milestone 1)**: shared `accept_ok`, naive hardening, relationship estimate wiring, and synthetic unit tests for must-haves and alternatives.
2. **Error and deadline handling**: 422/5xx in `play()`, a 35 s decision deadline, 409 late-send fix, `max_retries=0`, and an RFQ per-thread worker with a delayed-reply test on S02.
3. **Guard and prompt**: allow-listed prompt, structured claims with code-rendered figures, claim cap, dedupe and leak check, and the `notes` memory.
4. **Dossier and package seeds**.
5. **Hosted practice**, budgeted against 200 sessions per 24 h:
   - Run the 10 playable cases and read each replay.
   - Compare c_deal with c_best, and classify losses (wrong package, early accept, contradicted claim, timeout).
   - Check suppliers across profiles (squeezed family firm, pruned small account, large stable supplier, RFQ pair).
6. **Supplier simulator** as a `Sim._answer` replacement, only once replays show how suppliers behave.
7. **Latency and concurrency**:
   - Run `--parallel` up to 10 with the real clock.
   - Size the pool to the wave's cases and log queue delay.
   - Measure close-call latency and set `CLOSE_BEFORE_CAP_S` from it.
   - Re-read `seconds_left` before each decision.
   - Budget about 3-4 rounds per thread per wave [A].
8. **Fallbacks and restart**: LLM down, parse failure, 409, 422, 429, 5xx. Each must end in a valid deterministic move or an explicit walk.
   - Add a start-up reconcile for the final runner: list sessions, resume open ones, never open blindly, and run a single runner per key.
   - Test the 409 resume path. It depends on the `RUNNING` regex wording (`play.py:30`).
9. **Final rehearsal** from the final machine and network, with all cases parallel, finishing well inside 8 minutes. Re-run `arena data` after the Sunday release. Check the commit hash and that the README lists env var names only (`submission.md:5-15,31-38`).

**Success metrics**
- Mean hosted-practice case score against the naive baseline. Local naive scores 0.52 / 0.51 / 0.68 [A, carried over from an explorer and not re-run]. They only check plumbing.
- Zero must-have breaches and zero accepts with C ≥ C_alt.
- Contradicted-claim rate near 0.
- Fraction of cases closed before the cap.
- p95 decision latency under 35 s from the supplier reply, with zero timeouts.
- Zero unhandled exceptions across 10 parallel sessions.
- Gap C_deal − C_best per supplier profile.

## First milestone
Shared `accept_ok`, hardened `NaiveAgent` and `closing_move` (including picking the best RFQ thread), relationship estimate wiring, and unit tests on synthetic must-have and alternative cases. content.text:
The exploration is finished: 11 agents ran, the draft got 25 review issues, and the revised report below applies them. It was a read-only exploration, so no hosted calls were made, no quota was used and no `.env` file was read.

## What the challenge is
- **Docs:** the authoritative rules are in `brief/brief.md`, `brief/api.md` and `brief/submission.md` at the repo root. The data package is the root `data/` folder, with 24 tables in `data/world.sqlite` and 10,356 citable IDs in `data/facts.json`.
- **Score:** each case scores `clip((C_open − C_deal) / (C_open − C_best), 0, 1)`. Here C is total cost in euros. A wave is the mean of its case scores × 100, so the maximum is 500 over five waves. A deal that breaks a must-have scores 0.
- **Total cost** includes spend, the uncovered need priced at the fallback price, payment interest, freight, defects, an index adjustment and a supplier-health term.
- **Price alone misleads:** on the local case S03, a 12-month contract at the same price costs about 347k more than a 24-month one. A lower unit price can therefore lose.
- **Term sheets:** only buyer term sheets bind. Only the buyer closes, by accepting the supplier's standing sheet.
- **Claims:** at most 3 claims per message are checked, and an unknown ID or a wrong figure costs trust.
- **Limits:** 60 seconds per reply per thread, 10 rounds by default, and 8 minutes hard cap per wave in the final. Practice is limited to 200 sessions per 24 hours.
- **Final:** one attempt per case, no human in the loop, and the agent must not read `/events`, `/screen`, `/leaderboard` or `/results`.
- **Local sim:** it has only S01, S02 and S03. All three have empty must-haves and none is a `stabilise` or `secure_supply` case, so unit tests with synthetic cases have to cover must-haves and the relationship term.

## Gaps in the starter kit, confirmed in source
1. **Leaks and weak checks:** the LLM prompt includes the whole case JSON, with your alternative and cost rates. Nothing checks the output for leaks. `guard` doesn't cap claims, dedupe them or verify figures. `walk_away` is accepted unconditionally.
2. **Relationship term:** it is never passed to `total_cost`, so it is always 0.
3. **Closing:** `closing_move` accepts anything that passes the must-haves when the alternative is `none`. It also walks via `live_threads()[0]`, which ends a whole RFQ.
4. **Deadlines:** the LLM timeout is 45 seconds against a 60-second limit. No deadline is enforced, only a warning is logged.
5. **RFQ threads:** they are served one at a time, so the other threads' clocks run out while one is being sent.
6. **Errors:** a 422 or 5xx that survives the client's retries aborts the case, which then scores the alternative.
7. **Late sends:** a late send that gets a 409 is recorded as if it were a sent offer.

## Recommended architecture
Keep the existing stack and add a thin deterministic layer around one LLM call per turn. There is no multi-agent framework and no separate Closer role.
- **Prepare (once per case):** SQL builds a dossier of evidence cards and a justified-move calculation, plus one supplier cost estimate for the relationship term.
- **Turn (LLM):** it proposes term sheets, claims and the message body, and writes `notes` that feed the next turn. Code validates every sheet with `complete_offer`, must-haves, no-regression and a price floor. Claim figures are rendered from the dossier in code.
- **Accept or walk (code):** one shared `accept_ok` is used by `closing_move`, `guard` and `NaiveAgent`.
- **Fallback:** a precomputed move from a hardened `NaiveAgent`, with a 35-second decision deadline and `max_retries=0`.

## First milestone
Build the shared `accept_ok`, harden `NaiveAgent` and `closing_move` (including choosing the best RFQ thread), wire in the relationship estimate, and add unit tests on synthetic must-have and alternative cases. The result is an agent that can't score 0 by breaking a must-have and can't accept a deal worse than the alternative. It needs no hosted quota and no new LLM design.

After that: 422/5xx and 409 handling, the allow-listed prompt and tighter `guard`, the dossier, then hosted practice, then final rehearsal.

## Open questions for the organizers
- Is the quota really 200 per 24 hours? A remote source reportedly says there is none.
- What does a contradicted claim cost, and are `EV-`, `sup:` and `part:` IDs and meeting notes citable?
- What is the no-deal score, and how is C_best computed on hosted cases?
- What are the approval thresholds for supplier roles?
- Which governs when a contract disagrees with the case? S01's contract says EXW and 45 days, while the case fixes FCA and 60 days.
- Is prompt injection against supplier bots allowed?

## Caveats on the report
- **Re-run and unchecked items:** the final reviewer didn't re-run pytest or the naive agent's local scores (0.52, 0.51 and 0.68). The SQLite row counts and the S01 trace were also not re-checked in the last pass.
- **Hosted suppliers:** they are LLM-driven and their behaviour isn't documented, so supplier-interest inference stays a hypothesis until practice runs show how they respond.

1	**Procurement negotiation is a repeated business relationship under uncertainty.** Price matters, but so do supply continuity, quality, trust, internal approval, and whether both parties can deliver what they promise.
2	
3	For an agent, the challenge is to understand the commercial situation, make an appropriate move, and recognize when a person needs to take over.
4	
5	**1. What procurement actually involves**
6	
7	Procurement starts with a business need and continues through sourcing, contracting, delivery, performance management and eventual renewal or exit. Negotiation is one activity within that lifecycle. [CIPS procurement definition](https://1prd-dxp.cips.org/intelligence-hub/procurement/what-is-procurement).
8	
9	Consider a manufacturer buying a custom component:
10	
11	- Engineering needs the correct tolerances and material.
12	- Operations needs reliable delivery.
13	- Procurement wants competitive total cost.
14	- Finance cares about payment terms and working capital.
15	- Quality needs traceability and acceptable defect rates.
16	- The supplier needs margin, predictable demand and manageable production commitments.
17	
18	The negotiator must reconcile these interests. A cheaper component that causes production stoppages can be a worse purchase.
19	
20	**2. What the parties are negotiating**
21	
22	A deal is a package of interconnected terms.
23	
24	| Dimension | Buyer’s concern | Supplier’s concern |
25	|---|---|---|
26	| Price | Competitive cost | Adequate margin |
27	| Quantity | Avoid excess inventory | Economical production batches |
28	| Delivery | Availability and flexibility | Capacity and scheduling |
29	| Payment | Preserve cash | Receive cash predictably |
30	| Contract duration | Flexibility and continuity | Revenue certainty |
31	| Forecasts | Avoid overcommitment | Plan materials and capacity |
32	| Quality | Reliable performance | Feasible specifications |
33	| Risk allocation | Protection against failure | Avoid unmanageable obligations |
34	
35	This creates opportunities to trade across issues. A buyer might offer predictable volumes in exchange for a lower price, or faster payment in exchange for a discount.
36	
37	Presenting several packages of similar value to the buyer can also reveal what the supplier values most. This is the principle behind **multiple equivalent simultaneous offers**, or MESOs. [Harvard’s explanation](https://www.pon.harvard.edu/daily/dealmaking-daily/the-benefits-of-multiple-offers/).
38	
39	**3. The commercial concepts an agent needs**
40	
41	| Concept | Meaning | Example |
42	|---|---|---|
43	| Position | What a party explicitly asks for | “We need an 8% increase.” |
44	| Interest | The reason behind the position | Higher material costs or uncertain order volumes |
45	| Target | The preferred outcome | Keep the existing price |
46	| Reservation point | The least acceptable deal | Maximum acceptable total cost for a defined package |
47	| BATNA | Best alternative if agreement fails | Qualify another supplier or change the specification |
48	| ZOPA | The set of deals acceptable to both sides | Packages satisfying both parties’ limits |
49	| Authority | What the negotiator can commit to | May discuss pricing but cannot promise exclusivity |
50	
51	A BATNA must be realistic: an alternative supplier requiring six months of qualification may provide little leverage against a delivery needed next week. Harvard identifies alternatives as an important source of negotiating power. [Negotiation dynamics](https://www.pon.harvard.edu/tag/negotiation-dynamics/).
52	
53	**4. The lifecycle changes the negotiation**
54	
55	The following is a practical simplification of the broader [CIPS procurement cycle](https://1prd-dxp.cips.org/intelligence-hub/procurement/procurement-supply-cycle):
56	
57	| Stage | Main questions | Useful agent work |
58	|---|---|---|
59	| Define the need | What is essential? What can change? | Identify missing specifications and constraints |
60	| Understand the market | Who can supply? What are the alternatives? | Research suppliers and benchmark costs |
61	| Request offers | Are suppliers quoting comparable scopes? | Prepare RFQs and normalize quotations |
62	| Prepare negotiation | What are our priorities, limits and tradeable terms? | Build a mandate and evidence pack |
63	| Negotiate | What prevents agreement? Which package works? | Ask, propose, evaluate and track concessions |
64	| Approve and contract | Are the agreed terms complete and authorized? | Reconcile terms and route approvals |
65	| Deliver and manage | Did actual performance match the agreement? | Track delivery, quality and deviations |
66	| Renew or exit | Has the supplier earned more business? | Bring performance history into the next negotiation |
67	
68	Relationships accumulate history throughout this cycle. A supplier’s response today may reflect an unpaid invoice, an earlier broken forecast, or years of reliable collaboration.
69	
70	**5. Relationship and power**
71	
72	The appropriate approach depends on how much each party needs the other.
73	
74	For an easily replaceable standard item, competition and comparable quotations may dominate. For a specialized component with one qualified supplier, capacity, joint planning and continuity may matter more.
75	
76	A relationship has several dimensions:
77	
78	- **Dependability:** do both parties meet commitments?
79	- **Fairness:** are changes and concessions explained consistently?
80	- **Competence:** can the counterpart solve problems?
81	- **Transparency:** are relevant constraints disclosed?
82	- **History:** what happened in previous agreements?
83	
84	Close supplier relationships can support continuity and collaboration, especially with long-term suppliers. [CIPS supplier relationship guidance](https://cips-download.cips.org/fostering-collaboration-excelling-in-supplier-relationship-management).
85	
86	For an agent, relationship memory should record observable events: missed deliveries, resolved disputes, accepted concessions and fulfilled promises. A single “supplier sentiment score” loses much of that context.
87	
88	**6. Emotion and psychology**
89	
90	People negotiate on behalf of organizations, but experience the conversation personally. A supplier representative may worry about losing an account, appearing weak to a manager, or being blamed for an unprofitable agreement.
91	
92	Fisher and Shapiro identify five emotional concerns: **appreciation, affiliation, autonomy, status and role**. [Harvard’s discussion](https://www.pon.harvard.edu/daily/teaching-negotiation-daily/managing-emotions-in-negotiation-teaching-students-to-turn-emotions-into-an-opportunity-for-mutual-gain/).
93	
94	Applied to procurement:
95	
96	| Concern | Practical implication |
97	|---|---|
98	| Appreciation | Acknowledge the supplier’s explanation before challenging it |
99	| Affiliation | Frame shared problems around delivery, quality or continuity |
100	| Autonomy | Offer meaningful options and allow room for internal review |
101	| Status | Avoid language that humiliates or dismisses the counterpart |
102	| Role | Recognize that the salesperson may need someone else’s approval |
103	
104	An agent should distinguish **observations from interpretations**:
105	
106	> Observation: “The supplier repeated ‘final offer’ and requested a call.”  
107	> Possible interpretations: limited authority, frustration, a firm boundary, or a negotiation tactic.
108	
109	It should not confidently label the person “angry” or “dishonest” from a short email. Clarification is often more useful than psychological speculation.
110	
111	Another relevant effect is **anchoring**: the first number can influence subsequent offers. The agent therefore needs an independent valuation before reacting to the supplier’s opening price. [Harvard on counteroffers](https://www.pon.harvard.edu/daily/dealmaking-daily/how-to-counteroffer-in-business-negotiation/).
112	
113	**7. What a negotiation turn should accomplish**
114	
115	A turn is a meaningful move: a question, explanation, proposal, concession, rejection, acceptance or escalation. It may contain several messages and involve several people.
116	
117	A useful agent turn follows this sequence:
118	
119	1. **Interpret:** what changed in the latest response?
120	2. **Update:** which terms, constraints or assumptions changed?
121	3. **Evaluate:** does the current package meet our objectives and limits?
122	4. **Choose:** ask, counteroffer, offer alternatives, pause, escalate or close.
123	5. **Validate:** is the proposed move accurate and authorized?
124	6. **Communicate:** make one clear move with an understandable rationale.
125	7. **Record:** preserve the offer version, commitments and unresolved points.
126	
127	There is no universal ideal number of turns. A clarification can produce more value than another price concession. Repeated counteroffers with no new information may indicate that the parties need a different package or a human conversation.
128	
129	**8. An illustrative negotiation**
130	
131	Suppose a supplier requests an increase from €10 to €10.80 per component.
132	
133	| Turn | Move | Purpose |
134	|---|---|---|
135	| 1 | Buyer asks for cost drivers and effective date | Understand the request |
136	| 2 | Supplier cites material costs and unpredictable small orders | Surface underlying interests |
137	| 3 | Buyer questions the full increase and asks about larger batches | Test a possible trade |
138	| 4 | Supplier offers €10.30 with scheduled releases | Put a conditional package forward |
139	| 5 | Buyer checks inventory implications with operations | Validate the internal tradeoff |
140	| 6 | Buyer proposes €10.20, scheduled releases and a review mechanism | Exchange value across terms |
141	| 7 | Supplier requests approval internally | Resolve authority |
142	| 8 | Both parties confirm the complete package | Prevent ambiguous agreement |
143	
144	These numbers are illustrative. The lesson is that order predictability can change the economics of the deal.
145	
146	**9. What this means for an agent system**
147	
148	The system should maintain more than a chat transcript:
149	
150	| Context | What to retain |
151	|---|---|
152	| Commercial mandate | Objectives, limits, priorities and approval authority |
153	| Evidence | Quotes, benchmarks, specifications and source dates |
154	| Deal state | Current packages, conditions and unresolved terms |
155	| Counterpart context | Stated interests, known constraints and uncertain hypotheses |
156	| Relationship history | Performance, disputes, concessions and commitments |
157	| Workflow state | Awaiting supplier, internal review, approval or signature |
158	
159	Success should be measured through **total value, supply reliability, policy compliance, relationship outcomes and realized performance**. A signed agreement is only an intermediate result; the procurement outcome becomes clear when the promised goods or services are delivered.

84	
85	The buyer's world: supplier and part master data; three years of orders, goods receipts,
86	invoices and payments; quality notifications and quarterly scorecards (on-time delivery, PPM);
87	framework contracts and clauses; past RFQs and quotes; forecasts; supplier intel and news; past
88	negotiations, letters, e-mails, meeting and call notes; should-cost estimates; spend down to the
89	long tail; and monthly market indices (real public series, frozen at 2026-09-30).
90	
91	- **Every fact you can cite has an ID** `<type>:<id>[@period]`, e.g. `po:4500010001-10`,
92	  `idx:PPI-C2451@2026-08`, `sc:70110@2026Q3`, `ctr:4600070110#3.1`, `doc:…`.
93	- What moves a supplier is in the data - some of it only in the notes and e-mails. Some notes are
94	  just noise. The company and its suppliers are fictional.
95	- **Sunday 08:00: a second release** - market news, supplier letters and a memo from early October
96	  (`GET /v1/data` lists it). Hidden cases may cite its facts. Your agent should read it.
97	
98	## 5. How a negotiation works
99	
100	- **Round 0:** every supplier sends its quote e-mail at once, with a quote PDF.
101	- **Your message:** subject, body, up to 3 term sheets (each with a value for every negotiable
102	  field), the data IDs you rely on (IDs written in the body count too), optional text attachments.
103	- **The supplier answers by e-mail:** the role in charge writes; its standing term sheet; a status -
104	  `open`, `final_offer` (push further and it may walk), `agreed` (it offers exactly your terms; you
105	  still accept), `walked_away`, `no_bid`; signals (reply delay, quote validity); fields it left out;
106	  and how each data argument checked out. A supplier's reply can take **up to about a minute**;
107	  its time never counts against your 60 seconds.
108	- **Only you close a deal**, by accepting a supplier's standing term sheet. In **RFQ cases** 2-3
109	  suppliers run in parallel threads; accepting one ends the case.
110	- **Limits:** a round limit per thread (default 10 messages) and **60 seconds per message**, counted
111	  from the supplier's reply. A late message counts as
112	  a timeout: your last offer repeated, the supplier's patience drops; three in a row, or one after
113	  the last round, end the thread.
114	- **Unstated terms default to the supplier's standard terms** - listed in its quote PDF.
115	
116	**Documents** are rendered from the supplier's data, never invented: the quote PDF (read it before
117	you accept), a cost breakdown XLSX (ask; an open supplier sends one), an 8D report (quality), a
118	delivery schedule XLSX (logistics), and the order confirmation at the deal.
119	
120	**What counts:** **term sheets bind** - nothing else. **Data you cite is checked**: the reply says
121	`verified`, `contradicted` (a wrong figure or an unknown ID - it costs trust), `irrelevant` or
122	`duplicate`; whether a true argument moves the supplier, and how far, is the supplier's business.
123	**What you write is understood** - and has consequences, as it would with a person.
124	
125	## 6. The score: total cost in €
126	
127	Only the accepted term sheet scores. The case values it as the **total cost C** of covering your
128	**fixed need over a fixed horizon**, at the case's published rates. Every case states its
129	**category goal** - `stabilise`, `secure_supply`, `quality_first`, `leverage` or `routine` - and its
130	rates follow it. Reaching the goal is the skill.
131	
132	| Part of C | How |
133	|---|---|
134	| Price | committed units × unit price; units bought before a new price takes effect at the current price |
135	| Uncovered need | need the deal does not cover at the fallback price, plus the goal's fallback risk on it |
136	| Payment, freight, lead time | interest for paying earlier than your reference; freight by Incoterm; € per day beyond your need |
137	| Quality, other | expected defects at the committed PPM minus chargebacks; tooling; an index clause on the case's index path, plus the goal's index risk |
138	| The supplier's health | strategic and bottleneck goals only: € for every margin point the deal leaves the supplier below a sustainable margin (its margin on the cash it gets) |
139	
140	**Case score = (C_open − C_deal) / (C_open − C_best)**, clipped to 0…1. **C_open** is the best
141	opening quote. **C_best** is the cheaper of the best package any supplier in the case would ever
142	accept, with every valid lever applied, and your alternative - fixed per case, so good arguments
143	raise your score instead of moving the yardstick. **No deal** scores your alternative (0 if none);
144	some cases are best left without a deal. **A broken must-have** scores 0. **In the final** each
145	wave scores 0-100 (the mean of its case scores × 100, one decimal) and your **points so far** are the
146	sum of your wave scores - up to 500 after five waves. The formula is in `api.md`; `arena_kit.total_cost` computes C.
147	
148	**Example** (a `leverage` case: 3 % fallback risk) - need 4,000 a year for 2 years, interest 8%,
149	reference 60 days. The foundry asks €43.20 for a 24-month contract at 30 days net.
150	
151	| | Terms | C |
152	|---|---|---|
153	| C_open | €43.20, 30 days: 8,000 × 43.20 = 345,600, plus 30 days of early payment at 8% = 2,304 | €347,904 |
154	| Your deal | €41.60, 60 days: 8,000 × 41.60 = 332,800 | €332,800 |
155	| C_best (hidden) | €40.80, 90 days: 326,400, minus 30 days of interest saved = 2,176 | €324,224 |
156	| **Score** | (347,904 − 332,800) / (347,904 − 324,224) | **0.64** |
157	
158	The same €41.60 for 12 months covers half your need; the rest counts at the fallback price, say
159	€46.00, plus 3 %: C = €355,920 - worse than the opening, score 0.
160	
161	## 7. Rules
162	
163	1. **Not allowed:** humans in the loop during the Live Final, attacks on the service or on other
164	   teams, more than one API key per team - and agents that read the live feed during the Live
165	   Final: the event feed, the screen and the leaderboard (`/v1/events`, `/screen`, `/leaderboard`
166	   and their JSON).
167	2. **Everything else counts** - including weaknesses you find in our bots. Replays show how every
168	   score came about, and the jury may weigh that in the pitches. The goal is to convince a
169	   realistic supplier: that is what carries over to real negotiations.
170	3. **One attempt per case** in the final. An abandoned case is no deal.
171	4. **Code freeze at Sun 12:00.** Submit on ehl.gg: your repo (the agent and a README to run it), the
172	   commit hash, a short description and your pitch slides (`submission.md`). The final runs that
173	   commit, so your agent must be running and polling before 12:00. We check the top 10 for later
174	   pushes. Run your agent where you like, with your own LLM keys.
175	5. A supplier remembers only within a case; its history with your company is in the data.
176	
177	## 8. The weekend
178	
179	| When | What |
180	|---|---|
181	| Sat 10:00 | Kickoff and reveal: brief, data, kit, practice arena live |
182	| Sat 12:00-13:00 | Deep dive (ground floor, room on the signs): data, API, kit, Q&A - challenge selection closes 13:00 |
183	| Sat afternoon | Office hours at the Tacto table; practice all weekend |
184	| Sat ⟦TIME⟧ | Tacto stops answering for the night (Discord: https://discord.gg/hPwFfbWRV) |
185	| Sun 08:00 | **Sunday release:** new market news and letters (`/v1/data`) |
186	| Sun 09:00 | **Pre-flight:** one practice case through your final setup |
187	| Sun 12:00-~12:58 | **Code + slides freeze**, then the **Live Final** in 5 waves |
188	| Sun 13:00-14:30 | Top 10 pitch to the Tacto jury (5 min pitch + 2 min questions) |
189	| Sun 14:30 | Track winners and the two finalists announced |
190	| Sun 15:30 | Grand Final pitches (AudiMax) |
191	| Sun 16:30 | Awards |
192	
193	**The Live Final.** The hidden cases come in **5 themed waves**. The host shows each wave's
194	theme on the big screen, then starts the wave; its cases appear at the start, for all teams at once,
195	each in its own order, one session per case. **Each wave has a hard cap of 8 minutes:** threads
196	still open at the cap end with no deal (your alternative's score). Start your agent before the
197	first wave and keep it running: it plays all of a wave's cases **in parallel** (up to 10 open
198	sessions per key) - the kit's `arena run --set final` does that. The leaderboard shows your points
199	so far, wave by wave; replays and the suppliers' back office appear after the final. A case broken on our side is replayed.
200	
201	The hidden cases share the world, case types and rules of the practice set, with new suppliers and
202	settings. **Up to a third of them combine supplier types and case types that practice never shows**
203	- no new rules, but an agent that memorised the practice suppliers will meet strangers. Some cite
204	the Sunday release.
205	
206	## 9. Selection and prizes
207	
208	- **Top 10:** the 10 teams with the most points after the five waves pitch to our jury from 13:00:
209	  5 minutes + 2 minutes of questions. Every replay is open to the jury.
210	- **Track places 1-3** (open to all teams of the track): ⟦PLACEHOLDER - decided Sat morning:
211	  weighting of Live Final score vs. jury score, and the jury criteria (draft: approach,
212	  explainability, craft)⟧.
213	- **EHL Grand Final:** the best 2 of the 5 EHL finalist teams in this track go on to the Grand Final
214	  pitches. Finalist teams outside the top 10 are ranked by the Live Final score alone.
215	- **Ties:** points are points; an exact tie goes to more deals, then fewer rounds. At the top-10
216	  cut the jury looks at the score distribution. **Prizes:** €1,500 for 1st place, medals for the
217	  top 3, handed over by Tacto at the awards at 16:30.
218	
219	## 10. Tips
220	
221	- **Numbers come from code, the model writes.** Compute C for every term sheet; put figures from
222	  the data next to their IDs; let the LLM choose arguments and wording.
223	- **Read the supplier** before you argue: its notes, letters, news and quote remarks tell you what
224	  it is dealing with - and what will move it.
225	- **Read the quote PDF** before you accept: what you did not negotiate closes on its standard terms.
226	- **Ask, and offer alternatives.** Two or three term sheets show you what a supplier values.
227	- **Don't leak** urgency, a budget or a missing alternative. Don't take the first offer.
228	- **Plan your practice runs** (200 a day is for learning, not brute force) and **rehearse the
229	  final**: all hosted cases in parallel, from Sunday's machine and network, well inside 8 minutes.

Steps 1–7 are done. The hosted sandbox run (step 8) was blocked by your permission classifier, so I stopped there and did not work around it. The config works, but there is one bug to fix in `.env` and a key leak to clean up.

## Checklist

| Check | Result |
|---|---|
| `.env` variables | Set: `ARENA_URL=https://arena.tacto.ai`, `LLM_PROVIDER=openai`, `LLM_BASE_URL=https://api.openai.com/v1`, `LLM_MODEL=gpt-6-luna`, plus `ARENA_API_KEY` (32 chars) and `LLM_API_KEY` (164 chars). |
| `.env` ignored by git | Yes (`.gitignore` line 153). |
| `.env.example` on `main` | Clean, with placeholders. |
| Real keys in tracked files on `main` | None. |
| `gpt-6-luna` on OpenAI | Listed (HTTP 200, 129 models). |
| `arena me` | Works. Team "Boo 👾", 6 of 200 practice sessions used, best `case:P01` is 0.583. |
| Kit matches brief and context | Commands exist: `me`, `play`, `run`, `data`. The env names match. The client timeout is 180 s as `api.md` requires. |
| Local run: simulator plus LLM agent on S01 | Works end to end. `gpt-6-luna` answers in about 10–17 s per call. The final score was 0.37, so only the plumbing is verified. |
| Hosted sandbox run (`case:D01`) | **Not run.** Your permission classifier blocked it, so I stopped. Say the word, or add a Bash permission rule for it, if you want it. |

## Problems found
1. **`ARENA_DATA=data/package` points nowhere.** The folder doesn't exist, and the real data is at the repo-root `data/`. The LLM agent therefore runs without data unless you override it. Set `ARENA_DATA=../data` in `.env`, since you run from `starter-kit/`. I only overrode it in the shell for my test and didn't edit `.env`.
2. **Real keys exist in the local branch `entire/d085602-e3b0c4`.**
   - Its commit changes `.env.example` and contains a real Arena key and a real OpenAI key.
   - It also holds `full.jsonl` and `prompt.txt` files (session transcripts).
   - The remote has only `main`, so nothing is pushed. Never push this branch.
   - Rotate both keys, since they have lived in a git object. I didn't delete the branch because Entire owns it.
3. **The LLM reply parser is fragile.** In the S01 run, the model returned JSON followed by extra text, which raised `Extra data` and made the agent fall back to the naive move. Hardening `parse` in `agents/llm.py` is the first code fix I'd make, along with the milestone-1 safeguards from the report.

## Updated belief
The naive agent scored about 0.5 on local cases and the LLM agent scored 0.37 on S01. The parse failure and the fallback explain part of that. Don't assume the LLM agent beats the baseline yet.

The next step is your call. I'd fix `ARENA_DATA` and the parser, then start the milestone-1 work.
You can access the .env yourself change it yourself and let's start working and making a submission.

1	"""Read-only access to the data package: SQL, lookup by citable ID, documents, practice cases -
2	plus the Sunday release (new news, letters and a memo) once you have downloaded it."""
3	
4	import csv
5	import json
6	import os
7	import sqlite3
8	from functools import cached_property
9	from pathlib import Path
10	
11	MAX_ROWS = 200
12	RELEASE = "release-sunday"
13	
14	
15	class DataPackage:
16	    def __init__(self, root, release=None):
17	        """`root`: the unpacked package. `release`: the unpacked Sunday release (default: a
18	        `release-sunday` folder inside or next to the package, or ARENA_RELEASE), if present."""
19	        self.root = Path(root).expanduser().resolve()
20	        # facts.json holds every citable fact with the fields the arena checks claims against.
21	        own = self.root / "facts.json"
22	        facts = [own] if own.is_file() else [p for p in sorted(self.root.rglob("facts.json")) if RELEASE not in p.parts]
23	        self.facts = json.loads(facts[0].read_text(encoding="utf-8")) if facts else {}
24	        release = release or os.environ.get("ARENA_RELEASE")
25	        candidates = [Path(release).expanduser()] if release else [self.root / RELEASE, self.root.parent / RELEASE]
26	        self.release = next((p.resolve() for p in candidates if (p / "facts.json").is_file()), None)
27	        if self.release:  # new IDs only: nothing in the package changes
28	            self.facts |= json.loads((self.release / "facts.json").read_text(encoding="utf-8"))
29	        dbs = sorted(self.root.rglob("*.sqlite")) + sorted(self.root.rglob("*.db"))
30	        if not dbs and not facts:
31	            raise FileNotFoundError(f"no facts.json or .sqlite under {self.root}")
32	        self.db = None
33	        if dbs:
34	            self.db = sqlite3.connect(f"file:{dbs[0]}?mode=ro", uri=True, check_same_thread=False)
35	            self.db.row_factory = sqlite3.Row
36	            self.db.execute("PRAGMA query_only = ON")
37	
38	    def tables(self):
39	        """{table: {"columns": [...], "rows": n}}"""
40	        if self.db is None:
41	            return {}
42	        names = [r[0] for r in self.db.execute("SELECT name FROM sqlite_master WHERE type = 'table' ORDER BY name")]
43	        return {
44	            t: {
45	                "columns": [f"{c[1]} {c[2]}".strip() for c in self.db.execute(f'PRAGMA table_info("{t}")')],
46	                "rows": self.db.execute(f'SELECT count(*) FROM "{t}"').fetchone()[0],
47	            }
48	            for t in names
49	        }
50	
51	    def query(self, sql, params=(), limit=MAX_ROWS):
52	        if self.db is None:
53	            raise ValueError("this package has no SQLite file")
54	        if sql.lstrip().split(None, 1)[0].lower() not in {"select", "with"}:
55	            raise ValueError("read-only: SELECT or WITH statements only")
56	        cur = self.db.execute(sql, params)
57	        return [dict(r) for r in cur.fetchmany(limit)]
58	
59	    @cached_property
60	    def _ids(self):
61	        # A table's citable ID sits in its `id` column, else in its first column.
62	        index = {}
63	        for t, meta in self.tables().items():
64	            cols = [c.split()[0] for c in meta["columns"]]
65	            key = "id" if "id" in cols else cols[0]
66	            for row in self.db.execute(f'SELECT * FROM "{t}"'):
67	                value = row[key]
68	                if isinstance(value, str) and ":" in value:
69	                    index[value] = {"table": t, **dict(row)}
70	        for path in sorted(self.release.glob("data/*.csv")) if self.release else []:  # not in the SQLite
71	            with path.open(encoding="utf-8", newline="") as f:
72	                for row in csv.DictReader(f):
73	                    index[row["id"]] = {"table": path.stem, **row, "root": str(self.release)}
74	        return index
75	
76	    def lookup(self, ref):
77	        """The fact behind a citable ID (from facts.json, else its table row), or None."""
78	        return self.facts.get(ref) or self._ids.get(ref)
79	
80	    def ids(self, prefix):
81	        """All citable IDs starting with `prefix`, sorted, e.g. ids("idx:GP19-245113@")."""
82	        return sorted(i for i in self.facts.keys() | self._ids.keys() if i.startswith(prefix))
83	
84	    def document(self, ref):
85	        """A document's text by ID (row with a path or body column) or by path in the package."""
86	        row, base = self._ids.get(ref) or self.facts.get(ref), self.root
87	        if row:
88	            for col in ("body", "text", "content"):
89	                if row.get(col):

91	            base = Path(row.get("root") or self.root)
92	            ref = next((row[c] for c in ("path", "file") if row.get(c)), None)
93	            if ref is None:

95	        path = (base / ref).resolve()
96	        if not path.is_relative_to(base) or not path.is_file():
97	            raise FileNotFoundError(ref)
98	        return path.read_text(encoding="utf-8")

# Tacto Negotiation Arena - starter kit

A Python client for the arena API, two example buyer agents that negotiate by e-mail, helpers that
read the suppliers' documents and price a term sheet, a runner that plays many cases in parallel,
`arena-sim` - a local simulator of the arena's API - and a read-only MCP server over the data
package. Read the brief first
(`../brief/brief.md`); the full API is in `../brief/api.md`. Code: MIT.

## Quickstart - first agent on the board in 15 minutes

You need Python 3.12 and [uv](https://docs.astral.sh/uv/).

**1. Get your team's key** (one per team): open `https://arena.tacto.ai/apply`, enter your team name and a
contact e-mail, and show the match code it displays at the Tacto desk. Once an organiser approves,
the key appears **once** on that page - copy it and press "Got the key". Only that page (or its
link) shows it; lost it → ask the organisers to reset it. Keep it out of git.

```bash
cd starter-kit
uv sync --all-extras            # 2. install
cp .env.example .env            # 3. put ARENA_URL and your key (ARENA_API_KEY) into .env
uv run arena me                 # 4. your team and its practice quota
uv run arena cases              # 5. the practice cases (the 10 hosted ones are playable)
uv run arena play case:P01 -v   # 6. the naive agent negotiates one case
uv run arena board              # 7. you are on the practice leaderboard
```

Is the arena up? `curl $ARENA_URL/health`.

Step 6 prints the deal, your total cost `c_deal` against `c_open` and `c_best`, the case score,
and a **replay link**: every e-mail and the supplier's reasons for each move, in words. That is
the learning loop - play a practice case, read the replay, improve your agent, play
again. In practice your best score per case counts, so play a case again whenever your agent improves.
**Quota:** 200 practice sessions per team per rolling 24 hours. `arena play` and `arena run` print
how many are left; `arena run` plays only the hosted practice cases and stops starting new ones
once the quota is used up (a `429` there does not go away by retrying). Plan your runs.

**Now the LLM agent.** Download the data (`ARENA_DATA=data/package` in `.env`), choose a model in
`.env` (your own key), then:

```bash
uv run arena data                                          # unpacks data/package (and the Sunday release once public)
uv run arena play case:P01 --agent llm -v
uv run arena run --set practice --agent llm --parallel 8   # every hosted practice case, 8 at a time
uv run arena play case:D02 -v                              # the sandbox: 3 demo suppliers, no board
```

**Sunday 08:00:** run `arena data` again - it adds `data/release-sunday` (new news, letters, a
memo). `DataPackage` merges its facts and documents automatically; hidden cases may cite them.

## Hello World (local, 3 commands)

No key yet? Play a whole case against the local simulator - no network, no quota, no LLM costs.
The simulator's supplier is a plain script; the real ones are on arena.tacto.ai. After
`uv sync --all-extras` (step 2 above):

```bash
# terminal 1: the simulator (--data is optional: leave it out until you have run `arena data`)
uv run arena-sim serve --no-clock --data data/package
